(Image credit: French Air and Space Force) SHARE France has deployed the newly-developed firefighting kit aboard the A400M to support the assets suppressing the fires in the country’s southwest. The Airbus A400M conducted its first firefighting operation when an aircraft operated by the French Air and Space Force (FASF) dropped fire retardant over raging wildfires in France’s southwest on Jun. 25, 2026 . The move is part of the response to the massive fires that are raging in France. With the flames now closing in on the city of Bordeaux, Paris is saying the blazes could continue burning for months . Over 220,000 persons have been evacuated, according to the European Commissioner for crisis management Hadja Lahbib . Congratulations to the @Armee_de_lair and Sécurité Civile @SecCivileFrance for the first successful #A400M deployment to fight the wildfires in South West of France. On July 25, a FFrench Air & Space Force A400M has been equipped with a Roll-on/Roll-off (RO-RO) firefighting… pic.twitter.com/ArWdhwUzeR — Airbus Defence (@AirbusDefence) July 26, 2026 Airbus has been testing a modification kit to rapidly convert the A400M into a water bomber aircraft. This would allow the A400M to supplement traditional firefighting aircraft in case of high demand, such as with the current wildfires. A variety of assets is being employed in the operation, including France’s fleet of 12 Canadair CL-415 amphibian firefighting aircraft operated by the Sécurité Civile (Civil Protection) force; Aérospatiale AS 350B3 helicopters of the Bouches-du-Rhône Fire and Rescue Service (Pompiers13) equipped with the Bambi Bucket system and Dash-8 Q400-MR multirole tankers. According to Aerial Fire , six Australian Air Tractor AT-802 Fs from Aerotech Group and Xo Aviation have also been pressed into service for this effort. L’ A400M dans la lutte🔥. L’AAE avec @AirbusDefence , @CeamAwc , @SecCivileFrance et EMATT testent un kit de largage de retardant permettant de larguer jusqu’à 20t d’eau. 🎯 Appuyer les moyens spécialisés pour renforcer la lutte contre les incendies. 🔗 https://t.co/4H5AJFAfSB pic.twitter.com/XNbYfPZc3h — Armée de l’Air et de l’Espace (@Armee_de_lair) July 24, 2026 A400M firefighting conversion and capability The images released by Airbus and the FASF show the aircraft carrying the ‘A400M Firefighter Demo Kit Mk2’ and releasing the fire retardant. The press release by the Ministry of the Armed Forces suggested a single A400M being used in what it termed ‘Operation Sentinelle’, as a part of the continuing firefighting qualification testing being carried out with the Military Air Expertise Centre (CEAM), Airbus and the Directorate General for Civil Security and Crisis Management since 2024. The service’s 25-plus A400Ms are based at Air Base 123 (BA 123) in Orléans. A French A400M military plane dumped retardant over Lacanau’s wildfire-hit forest land, joining firefighting efforts for the first time pic.twitter.com/iLx4gMmyVI — Reuters (@Reuters) July 25, 2026 Indonesia too has been considering ordering firefighting kits for two of its own A400Ms from Airbus. Airbus said in November 2025 that the roll-on/ roll-off (Ro-Ro) modular firefighting kit allows the A400M to be rapidly converted into a water bomber aircraft, capable of dropping up to 20,000 litres (20 tons) of fire retardant or water in a single pass. The Ro-Ro kit can be rapidly installed in the cargo hold without any permanent airframe modification. The tanks, which discharge the fire retardant through the rear ramp, can be refilled in under 10 minutes by standard ground pumps. The company previously conducted trials and certification of this firefighting module in April 2025 at Nîmes-Garons. The performance of the kits firefighting ability was separately assessed by Entente-Valabre’s Test and Research Centre (CEREN). Une première mondiale, rendue possible en seulement quinze jours grâce à la mobilisation exemplaire de la Sécurité civile, des armées et d’Airbus. Merci à toutes celles et ceux qui l’ont rendue possible.… pic.twitter.com/XpA7afWFXb — Sébastien Lecornu (@SebLecornu) July 25, 2026 The statement from Airbus said the so-called “cup grid tests” demonstrated “the accurate distribution and concentration of retardant upon reaching the ground,” with the modified A400M flying at altitudes below 30 meters (98 feet) and speeds around 230 km/hour (125 knots). Canadair CL-415s at the Air Base 123 in Orléans. (Image Credit: French Air and Space Force) The French Ministry of the Armed Forces added that the 20 ton fire-retardant drop capability is “equivalent to two drops by Dash aircraft.” The Ministry further explained how the A400M would be used in the firefighting role: “The aircraft would operate upstream of the flames. Its use would thus contribute to providing ad hoc support to specialized resources in this field, particularly those of the Civil Security service: Canadair and Dash aircraft. This new capability would not change the aircraft’s structure, which would retain its military capabilities.” Impresionante, gracias por vuestra lucha. pic.twitter.com/3y1g6UfmS1 — Capitán General de los Tercios (@capTercio) July 26, 2026 While the firefighting kit has now been used operationally, the trial phase will still continue and put the kit through the “necessary […] testing and qualification.” The statement further added “The CEAM (Air Warfare Experimentation Center) is fully committed to this effort, particularly in the operational performance evaluation phases and the formulation of conclusions.” Le lundi 29 juin 2026 sur la base aérienne 106 “capitaine Michel Croci” les Air tractor décollent de la base (Image Credit: French Air and Space Force) France’s former defense minister and current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described the first real-life fire retardant drop by the A400M as “A world first, made possible in just fifteen days thanks to the exemplary mobilization of Civil Security, the armed forces, and Airbus.” He further added: “Thank you to all those who made it possible. This new capability now strengthens the aerial resources already deployed in the field.” Le combat continue, force à ceux qui sont en pleine bataille encore aujourd’hui ! Il faudra s’en rappeler une fois le calme revenu. pic.twitter.com/XSc1l3UroF — Thomas Pesquet (@Thom_astro) July 27, 2026 Europe mobilizes Interestingly, at least one of the two Czech S-70 Firehawks that Prague ordered in November 2025 also operated in suppressing the fires in the village of La Temple, in the Gironde department in southwestern France’s Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. The Fire and Rescue Service of the Czech Republic said on X that “The Czech air firefighting module in France today helped protect the village of Le Temple, which was practically surrounded by flames. The fire in the Gironde department affected around 30,000 ha.” 🚁Český modul leteckého hašení ve Francii dnes pomáhal chránit obec Le Temple, kterou plameny prakticky obklíčily. 🔥 Požár v departementu Gironde zasáhl okolo 30 000 ha. The Spanish Ministry of the Interior has informed that four Canadair CL-415s (two each from Italy and Greece), along with 14 and 33 specialist personnel, respectively, are in various stages of beginning firefighting operations. Greece additionally reported sending a C-27J Spartan to Spain to support the operations. The aircraft landed there for technical stops while dousing fires in the Fontainebleau forest in Seine-et-Marne region. “At very short notice, the military was able to refuel the aircraft, allowing them to quickly resume their missions,” said a statement. 📍 Sud de la France | Les armées aux côtés de la population 🔥 ➡️ Face à cette crise majeure, les armées sont mobilisées en appui des forces de sécurités intérieures et des services de secours engagés contre les incendies. 🎯 Au plus près des zones sinistrées, elles déploient… pic.twitter.com/vCWIb4m9nx — Armée française – Opérations militaires (@EtatMajorFR) July 26, 2026 Other FASF bases supporting the firefighting efforts include BA 701 Salon-de-Provence in the Southeast, which is “positioned close to the most exposed areas” and “hosted a water-bombing helicopter from the Bouches-du-Rhône Fire and Rescue Service (SDIS) throughout the summer season.” Further west, BA 106 in Bordeaux-Mérignac reactivated its water-bombing base on Jun. 24, as it was “located in the immediate vicinity of the most vulnerable forest areas.” En cette période d’épreuve, je salue l’engagement exemplaire de celles et ceux qui sont mobilisés face aux incendies. https://euobserver.com/238065/listen-aft.text: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below: Yesterday, several dozen people gathered in Valletta to demand justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese investigative journalist who was murdered in 2017. Nine years after her murder, the person who allegedly ordered it has still not been convicted. How can such impunity still exist in Europe? Daphne Caruana Galizia was one of Malta’s best-known investigative journalists. She was killed on 16 October 2017 when a bomb planted under her car exploded. She had exposed numerous corruption scandals involving Malta’s political establishment, including revelations linked to the Panama Papers. Read more European Parliament’s Metsola on Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict: ‘We will not give up, we will not give in’ And at the time of her death, she was investigating alleged corruption involving businessman Yorgen Fenech, who would later become the main suspect in her murder. But nine years later, Fenech has just been acquitted by a Maltese jury, after a trial that lasted several years. On the second of September, the jury found that his guilt had not been established beyond reasonable doubt. The verdict was met with anger from Daphne Caruana Galizia’s family and supporters, who have continued to call for those responsible for her murder to be held accountable. Reporters Without Borders deplored that, nine years after the assassination, the Maltese authorities had still failed to identify and convict the person who ordered the killing. Their anger is fueled by elements pointing at Fenech’s guilt. One of the key pieces of evidence came from Melvin Theuma, Fenech’s former driver and an intermediary in the murder. Theuma told the court that he had been paid one hundred fifty thousand euros, to organise the assassination. He also provided text messages and recordings involving Fenech, which prosecutors argued showed that Fenech had ordered the murder and was trying to make evidence disappear. But Fenech ha s consistently denied any involvement and has maintained his innocence. Read more Caruana Galizia family urges EU not to fund ‘corrupt’ gas pipeline As for the other people involved in the murder, five people have been convicted for their roles in preparing the assassination or supplying and planting the bomb used to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia. Melvin Theuma, who admitted organising the murder, was granted immunity from prosecution in exchange for his testimony. Now, what happens next? Read more Greece, Cyprus and Hungary worst offenders on press freedoms in EU The Maltese prosecution service has announced that it intends to appeal the jury’s decision regarding Jorgen Fennech. But in order to do so, it first has to identify a serious legal error in the proceedings. According to the Times of Malta , prosecutors could challenge a decision by the judge not to tell jurors that Fenech had requested a presidential pardon shortly after his arrest in November 2019. For now, the appeal has not yet been formally filed. Prosecutors still have a few days to do so. So what can the European Union actually do in a case like this? The investigation and prosecution of the murder remain in the hands of the Maltese authorities. The EU cannot take over the case. What it can do is strengthen protections for journalists and the rule of law. The European Media Freedom Act, which entered into force last year, strengthens the protection of journalistic sources and, in principle, prohibits the use of spyware against journalists. The EU has also adopted new rules against so-called SLAPPs — lawsuits designed to intimidate journalists or drain them financially. This is particularly relevant in Daphne Caruana Galizia’s case. When she was alive, she was literally harassed with SLAPPs. And the tradition goes on: just a few days ago, Yorgen Fenech reportedly threatened several media outlets with legal action if they published what he considers to be false allegations — namely, that the jurors who acquitted him had been bribed. Daphne Caruana Galizia’s case is not the only example of how difficult it can be to bring those responsible for the murder of journalists to justice. In 2018, Slovak journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée, Martina Kušnírová, were also murdered. Read more Will verdict in killing of Slovak journalist be a rare sign of hope? And in that case too, a suspected mastermind has been identified but has not been convicted. Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s assassination, her murder therefore remains a major test for Malta — and for Europe’s ability to protect journalists and ensure that those who attack them are held accountable. https://globalvoices.org/2026/10/03/how-.text: How a farmers’ protest in Bucharest was inflated online, then hijacked A real economic grievance became fuel for pre-existing anti-system narratives in Romania Written by Guest Contributor Read this post in عربي , Yorùbá , English Posted 3 October 2026 Thumbnail image of the YouTube video ‘Violențe la protestul oierilor din Piața Victoriei’ on the September 15, 2006 protests in Bucharest, Romania, by Digi24HD. English translation of the caption: ‘Violence at the protest on Victoriei Square. Clashes with the gendarmes, tear gas used.’ Fair use. This post by Matei Vrabie and Calin Georgia of Funky Citizens , a Romanian NGO working at the intersection of good governance and active citizenship, is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy .” With this spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here . On September 15, several hundred to more than a thousand shepherds, livestock breeders and other farmers gathered in Victoriei Square, in front of the Romanian government’s headquarters in Bucharest, to protest an EU-wide ban on live sheep and goat exports , extended until the end of 2026 after outbreaks of small ruminant plague and sheep pox. They demanded compensation for culled animals and for crops lost to drought. Organisers had called on protesters to bring sheep, tractors and hay bales to the square, but restrictions prevented live animals and heavy machinery from entering the demonstration area. The demonstration began peacefully before 10:00 a.m. By the afternoon, some protesters had pushed through police barriers and were throwing stones, bottles and pieces of curb; gendarmes responded with tear gas. According to the Bucharest Gendarmerie, 24 people needed medical attention that evening, including 10 gendarmes, four of whom were hospitalised, and 47 people were taken to police stations . President Nicușor Dan and interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan both condemned the violence . Livestock breeders’ associations said people who were not farmers had joined the crowd, and the Prefect of Bucharest said that “sheep farmers don’t organise themselves like this.” That is what happened on the street. What happened online, alongside and ahead of it, is the subject of a new report by Funky Citizens , the Bucharest-based civic organisation where I research digital manipulation and disinformation. Together with colleagues, we analysed 1,186 public Facebook posts and 100 TikTok videos published in Romanian on September 14 and 15, tracking which narratives about the protest circulated, how identical or near-identical wording moved between pages seconds apart, and what language accompanied calls for mobilisation. The clearest finding does not concern the violence. It concerns the night before. Between 7:00 and 7:15 p.m. on September 14, dozens of Facebook pages republished, almost word for word, a message claiming that “almost 200,000 farmers” were expected in Victoriei Square the next day. The following day, according to press reports, over 3,000 people showed up. Using a 300-second window to flag identical or near-identical wording published by different pages, we mapped the resulting coordination network. Roughly 90 percent of the 2,253 account pairs in the final network, built over the full two days, had already formed within those 15 minutes on the evening before the protest even began. Distribution of posts and public attention. Graph by Funky Citizens, used with permission. By 3:30 p.m. on September 15, the network comprised 160 accounts and 12 distinct texts multiplied across it. The structure was highly concentrated: two clusters of 50 accounts each, built around two near-identical versions of the “200,000 farmers” message, accounted for 100 of the 160 accounts and close to 90 percent of all connections. The most visible nodes we could identify by name, pages such as Case de Vis, femina.ro and ROL.ro, are content-aggregation and syndication pages, not overtly political ones. Republishing identical text within seconds is, by definition, coordinated distribution in a technical sense. It does not, on its own, establish who organised it or why; our dataset does not permit conclusions about intent. Around this coordination, four narrative threads ran through the corpus. One concerned the farmers’ concrete economic demands: halting slaughter, resuming exports, fair prices. A second covered the escalation with the Gendarmerie, split between accounts blaming protesters for forcing police lines and accounts blaming the police, alongside a recurring claim that “provocateurs” had been planted in the crowd. A third thread politicised the protest outright, built around AUR leader George Simion’s calls for calm and for the Gendarmerie to show restraint , and around disputes over whether his intervention helped or undermined the farmers’ cause. A fourth thread, more detached from the day’s events, covered structural problems in Romanian agriculture, from delayed EU funding for machinery to the shift toward no-till farming. Chronological 3D dissemination network. Graph by Funky Citizens, used with permission. References to the European Union split into two distinct registers. Sixty-seven posts mentioned Brussels or the EU in connection with the protest. Some described concrete negotiations over the export ban with the European Commission; others recast the EU as an adversary, with formulations such as “Europe’s goal is to leave us without animals, without livestock farming, without agriculture in Romania,” or claims that “the EU would want to starve Romania.” We separately tracked two Telegram channels previously documented by the “Elie Wiesel” National Institute and by the security think tank GLOBSEC , as part of pro-Kremlin propaganda networks active in Romania and Moldova. Their framing of the protest shifted within hours. At 11:56 a.m., one channel described the demonstration, listing the farmers’ demands. By 2:06 p.m., a second channel had moved to warning that “the usurpers” would use the protest to stage “provocations, then escalation, then a state of emergency.” By 4:03 p.m., after the clashes, the same channel pivoted again to attacking how television stations covered the confrontation. A similar shift, from grievance to provocation-and-escalation to media distrust, recurred in posts using explicit mobilisation language, including calls to “occupy Bucharest” and declarations that “the REVOLUTION has begun.” On TikTok, where we sampled 100 videos from 34 accounts under the hashtag #protest, the same divide surfaced. Thirty-one videos mentioned the Gendarmerie directly in their description, and the single most shared video, announcing renewed clashes and dozens of arrests, drew nearly 30,000 interactions on its own. None of this tells us who organised the protest, or who benefited from inflating expectations about it. What the data show is a pattern familiar across Romania and the wider region: a real economic grievance, amplified within hours by dense clusters of accounts republishing identical text, and folded into pre-existing narratives about stolen elections, an illegitimate government and a “system” to be confronted. Distinguishing the farmers’ protest from its online amplification, and the amplification from any deliberate political instrumentalisation, is not a footnote to understanding what happened in Victoriei Square. It is the story. This post is part of Advox , a Global Voices project dedicated to protecting freedom of expression online. https://www.dw.com/en/un-peacekeeping-mi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OtM2 Prefer DW on Google Friday's failed US draft resolution would have rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination. Image: FADEL SENNA/AFP Advertisement The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires. The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century. Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory, The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic. US and Russia wield vetoes On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component. Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory. Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination. The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained. "We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said. "The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of ⁠the draft," ​he added. The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before. "Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote. https://www.economica.net/presedintele-n.text: Home - News - Președintele Nicușor Dan, despre negocierile de pace pentru Ucraina: Am stabilit de principiu să fim parte ”Evident, poziţia noastră cu privire la Marea Neagră este cunoscută şi interesul de a o proteja cu toate elementele şi militare, şi diplomatice, şi de informaţii. Iar în ceea ce priveşte recentele negocieri cu privire la războiul din Ucraina, a existat, cum am spus, o discuţie de principiu. Am stabilit de principiu că e util ca Europa să fie parte din aceste discuţii”, a precizat şeful statului, citat de News.ro. El a mai afirmat că ”s-a stabilit în mod unanim că aceste discuţii nu trebuie să aibă de a face cu arhitectura de securitate a Europei, ci doar strict cu războiul din Ucraina, inclusiv cu garanţiile de securitate din faza de după terminarea războiului”. ”Şi pentru Uniunea Europeană şi pentru Coaliţia de Voinţă s-a stabilit cine să participe la aceste discuţii, urmând ca, dacă ele vor avea loc, urmând ca ulterior deciziile să fie luate în interiorul celor două organisme, Uniunea Europeană şi Coaliţia de Voinţă.
